read: partial: pp.1-9 (abstract, introduction, related work, method, experiments, conclusion, limitations) read in full; Appendix A.7 (expert validation of the verifier, p.14) read; the other appendices, fine-grained results and prompts (pp.14-23) skimmed.
venue_now: arXiv 2606.03660v2 [cs.AI], 3 Jun 2026 (page 1 stamp); no venue shown (ACL-style layout with a Limitations section)
what_it_is: ChemCoTBench-V2 is a rule-verifiable, process-level benchmark for chemical reasoning: 5,620 samples in 18 reporting tasks across molecular understanding, molecule editing, molecular optimization and reaction prediction, drawn from public chemistry databases and task pools (pp.1, 3). Models must answer in expert-refined templates whose fields expose intermediate chemical states; those fields are checked by deterministic RDKit rules (Type-I), by agreement with step-level reference traces (Type-II) and, for open-ended optimization, by oracle predicates, with no LLM judge (pp.3-5). The reference traces are generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 conditioned on the ground-truth answer and kept only if they pass the rule checks (p.3). Outcome, template adherence and step-wise verifier correctness are reported separately for eight frontier LLMs, and the verifier agrees with three expert chemists' labels on 300 steps at Cohen kappa 0.74 (pp.5-7, 14).
domain: chemistry (molecular structure, molecule editing, molecular optimization, reaction prediction); not engineering
size: 5,620 samples, 18 reporting tasks (31 implementation subtasks), four task families (pp.1, 3, 14); eight LLMs evaluated (p.5)
source_of_items: public chemistry databases and task-specific pools, sanitised and canonicalised with RDKit; editing items recast from real reactant-product changes (p.3)
has_gold_traces: yes, for closed-answer tasks: verified step-level reference traces generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 with access to the ground-truth answer and the fixed template, kept only if they pass outcome, template and intrinsic rule checks (p.3); open-ended optimization uses oracle predicates instead (p.5)
evaluation: step-level or process, deterministic: Layer 1 final-answer metrics (exact match, MAE, Tanimoto similarity, accuracy, success rate), Layer 2 template adherence (rule checks on fields and their consistency), Layer 3 step-wise verifier correctness (Type-I intrinsic RDKit checks, Type-II agreement with the reference trace, five oracle predicates for optimization); no LLM judge (pp.4-5)
human_validation: Chemistry experts pruned the LLM-induced template fields (p.3); conflicts in reference construction were inspected manually or excluded (p.3); three expert chemists independently labelled 300 randomly sampled step-level traces as correct, incorrect or ambiguous, and the deterministic verifier matched the majority label on 87.4% of step judgments (Cohen kappa 0.74), against 90.1% (kappa 0.79) between humans (App. A.7, p.14).
contamination_measures: none for pretraining contamination (the items come from public databases); answer-leaking metadata is stripped and condition-ranking labels are shuffled against shortcuts (p.3)

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in the May paper. Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity (it is outside engineering). Its design is the closest to EngTrace's verification stack among the candidates: deterministic checks of intermediate states against reference traces instead of an LLM judge, outcome and step correctness reported separately, and the verifier validated against expert step labels (pp.4-5, 14); its title, 'verifiable process-level evaluation', is close to EngTrace's 'verifiable process supervision'. EngTrace must therefore confine any claim about deterministic step verification to engineering and state the differences: ChemCoTBench-V2 checks the fields of a template the model is forced to fill (p.3), not free-form traces; its references are generated by LLMs that saw the answer (p.3), not computed by template code; its items are static and public; and its expert check covers 300 steps labelled by three chemists, where EngTrace's covers 300 traces labelled by 15 experts.

suggested_wording: In chemistry, ChemCoTBench-V2 (Guo et al., 2026) checks the intermediate states that models enter into fixed templates with deterministic rule verifiers and verified reference traces rather than an LLM judge, although its reference traces are themselves generated by LLMs given the answer.
facts_to_cite: 5,620 samples in 18 reporting tasks across molecular understanding, molecule editing, molecular optimization and reaction prediction (pp.1, 3).
Items are drawn from public chemistry databases and task-specific pools and sanitised with RDKit (p.3).

Models must answer in expert-designed templates whose fields expose intermediate chemical states; the templates were induced from natural chain-of-thought traces by an LLM and pruned by chemistry experts (p.3).

Step-level reference traces are generated by GPT-5.4 and Claude-Opus-4.7 from the task input, the ground-truth answer and the template, and are kept only if they pass the outcome, template and intrinsic rule checks (p.3).

Three signals are reported separately: Layer 1 final-answer metrics, Layer 2 template adherence, and Layer 3 step-wise verifier correctness (Type-I intrinsic RDKit checks, Type-II agreement with the reference trace, oracle predicates for optimization) (pp.4-5).

Three expert chemists labelled 300 sampled step-level traces: the verifier matched the adjudicated label on 87.4% of step judgments (Cohen kappa 0.74), against 90.1% (kappa 0.79) between humans (App. A.7, p.14).
Across eight frontier LLMs, models often complete the template while failing step checks, or answer correctly while an intermediate state fails a check (pp.2, 5-7).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: deterministic step-level verification against reference traces (pp.4-5); separate reporting of answer and step correctness (p.2); expert validation of the verifier with chance-corrected agreement (p.14); the argument against LLM judges and reward models for process evaluation (pp.1-2). Lacks: engineering content (chemistry); generated instances (static items from public databases, p.3); code-derived gold traces (its references are LLM-generated and answer-conditioned, p.3); evaluation of unconstrained traces (fixed templates, p.3); contamination measures. Unlike EngTrace it needs no residual judge, because every template field is rule-checkable.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. Must or should is a judgment call: it is outside engineering, so a revision that confines its novelty claims to engineering could treat it as should; I rate it must because it is the nearest verification design to EngTrace's and a reviewer who knows it would ask for the comparison. The search note's description is accurate; add that the reference traces are LLM-generated with access to the ground truth (p.3) and that the model's output format is fixed by a template (p.3). It presents itself as V2; the text cites Li et al. (2025), 'Beyond chemical QA: evaluating LLM's chemical reasoning with modular chemical operations', by overlapping authors (p.2 and references), presumably V1, without naming it ChemCoTBench.
